text:
8.1

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-85749
MailWatch: IDOR lets any authenticated user release or delete another tenant's quarantined mail

MailWatch for MailScanner is a web-based front-end to MailScanner. Prior to 1.2.27, any authenticated MailWatch user, including the U/user, D/domain-admin, and H/host roles, can release to inbox or permanently delete the quarantined mail of any other user or domain by supplying an arbitrary message `id` to `mailscanner/quarantine_action.php`. The action path calls `quarantine_list_items()` in `mailscanner/functions.php`, which selects from `maillog` by the supplied identifier without the per-role `global_filter` applied by listing and read views. The action requires a valid session and CSRF token, but the caller can submit a token from the caller's own session; ownership of the requested message is never checked. Message identifiers are enumerable, allowing a low-privilege user to invoke `quarantine_release()` or `quarantine_delete()` for other users' or domains' quarantined messages, force-delivering mail held by the quarantine or permanently deleting it. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.27.

title: CVE-2026-61572 - AVideo-Encoder: unauthenticated full-response server-side request forgery
text:
8.6

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-61572
AVideo-Encoder: unauthenticated full-response server-side request forgery

AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Before the initial remediation attempt in 8.1.0, `url_get_contents` in `objects/functions.php` accepts caller-controlled destinations after only `FILTER_VALIDATE_URL` syntax validation, without rejecting private, loopback, or link-local addresses, and disables TLS peer verification. `Login::isLogged` reauthenticates using the attacker-settable `encoder_aVideoURL` cookie together with arbitrary nonempty `encoder_user` and `encoder_pass` cookies, and `Login::run` stores the raw fetched body in `result`. The unauthenticated `objects/login.json.php` endpoint returns that session object, enabling full-response exfiltration through a supplied `siteURL`; its `Streamer::isURLAllowed` gate allows all sites when the operator allowlist is empty, the default. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read internal HTTP and HTTPS responses, including cloud instance-metadata credentials, and reach internal TCP services. A further pre-authentication FTP variant in `view/youtubeDl.json.php` routes an ftp `videoURL` into `FTPDownloader`; `parseFtpUrl` in `objects/FTPDownloader.php` accepts its host and port for `ftp_connect`. This also enables requests to internal FTP services. Untrusted self-signed HTTPS certificates are accepted, and no account or operator interaction is required. Version 8.1.0 contains an initial remediation attempt that removes raw-response reflection and adds destination checks, but private-network exemptions and login TLS-verification defaults leave complete remediation of the described internal-network and TLS variants unresolved.

title: CVE-2026-61567 - AVideo-Encoder: unauthenticated command execution through streamer login trust
text:
10.0

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-61567
AVideo-Encoder: unauthenticated command execution through streamer login trust

AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, the live-streaming endpoint `view/videosListToLive.php` accepts an attacker-named streamer in `webSiteRootURL`, calls `Login::run` in `objects/Login.php`, and trusts the returned JSON as session state. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can host an HTTP service reachable by the encoder can self-grant `isLogged` and `canStream` without legitimate credentials. The endpoint requires only nonempty `playlists_id` and `APISecret` values; `APISecret` is forwarded rather than checked against a stored secret. This path never calls `Streamer::isURLAllowed` and therefore works regardless of the operator's streamer allowlist. It fetches a second attacker-controlled video-list response and interpolates `videos[].path` without shell argument escaping into `ffprobe` and `ffmpeg` commands passed to `exec`; `isAudio` calls `isVideo` to reach the `ffprobe` command. Paths containing shell delimiters execute arbitrary operating-system commands as the web-server user. The request filter does not inspect the video-list JSON. This can disclose database and stored streamer credentials, compromise the upstream platform using those credentials, modify files owned by the web-server user, establish persistence, and deny encoder service. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.0.

text:
10.0

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-61564
AVideo-Encoder: unauthenticated installer PHP code injection

AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, the unauthenticated installer endpoint `install/checkConfiguration.php` assembles `videos/configuration.php` by interpolating request parameters, including `webSiteRootURL`, into single-quoted PHP string literals without escaping. An attacker can terminate a literal and inject PHP that executes as the web-server user when the generated, directly requestable file is loaded. Exploitation requires `videos/configuration.php` to be absent, as on every fresh deployment or after the file is removed or moved; an existing file blocks this endpoint. The supplied `systemRootPath` must contain index.php and a connection using `databaseHost`, `databaseUser`, and `databasePass` must succeed, but the attacker can point those parameters to their own database server and needs no target credentials. The write location is also derived from `systemRootPath` without a base-directory constraint. This permits arbitrary command execution, reading and overwriting files owned by the web-server user, persistent PHP code, and control over stored database connection settings. The endpoint additionally interpolates request values into streamer and configuration INSERT statements, creating a secondary SQL-injection sink. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.0.

title: CVE-2026-118669 - OAuthLib: Token grants can use attacker-supplied client_id for authorization after authenticating a different client
text:
8.4

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-118669
OAuthLib: Token grants can use attacker-supplied client_id for authorization after authenticating a different client

OAuthLib is an implementation of the OAuth request-signing logic for Python 3.6+. Prior to 4.0.0, the client_credentials and Resource Owner Password Credentials token grant handlers can authenticate request.client as one confidential client while retaining an attacker-supplied request.client_id for validate_grant_type and validate_scopes. A lower-privilege authenticated client can therefore cause grant and scope authorization to use another client's identity when an application validator relies on the documented client_id argument, potentially issuing tokens with unauthorized grants or scopes. Validators that authorize exclusively from request.client may not be affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.0.0.

text:
8.2

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-118664
decode-uri-component: Denial of service via quadratic replacement of percent-encoded runs

decode-uri-component provides a more robust alternative to decodeURIComponent. Prior to 0.5.1, decodeUriComponent in index.js falls back to customDecodeURIComponent after native decoding throws, and the fallback collects every distinct percent-encoded run before performing a full-string regular-expression replacement for each entry. Malformed input containing many distinct runs can therefore make both the number of replacements and the scanned input length grow together, causing quadratic CPU consumption and blocking the Node.js event loop; request-body inputs can reach the demonstrated size, while ordinary URL header limits reduce the practical delay. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.1.

The China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Volt Typhoon has been attributed to a now-disrupted covert access network dubbed Silent Train that has been put to use for zero-day exploitation and strategic access.

"First identified in late 2023, Silent Train uses rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise infrastructure," Lumen Technologies Black Lotus Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It employs anti-forensic techniques, compartmentalized operations, and post-operation cleanup to minimize detection and attribution."

Its main purpose is to facilitate critical attack phases like vulnerability exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration, and to maintain continued access to victim environments. The activity stands out for two main reasons -

It singled out entities that could provide scalable access to downstream customers, sensitive networks, or strategic programs.
It targeted endpoint management platforms, network management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators, and control plane technologies that play a crucial role within enterprise environments.

Hundreds of victims have been identified across telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms, and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, and emergency services.

Volt Typhoon (aka Bronze Silhouette, Insidious Taurus, UNC3236, Vanguard Panda, and Voltzite) is the moniker assigned to a China-linked state-sponsored group known for its targeting of critical infrastructure networks, particularly communications, energy, transportation, and water and wastewater systems sectors.

Known to be active since at least 2021, the threat actor was previously observed exploiting a file upload vulnerability in Versa Director as a zero-day (CVE-2024-39717) to deliver a bespoke web shell called VersaMem designed to harvest credentials and enable access to downstream customers.

The latest findings from Black Lotus Labs show that the security flaw was one among four confirmed zero-day campaigns the threat actor has conducted through Silent Train. The remaining three vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 - A set of insecure deserialization and command injection vulnerabilities in N-able N-central.
CVE-2026-20127 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller
CVE-2026-16812 - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator

Separately, Volt Typhoon is also suspected to have taken advantage of a likely zero-day vulnerability in Quest KACE before it was patched in October 2025. The campaign is estimated to have impacted more than 30 victims.

"Silent Train is built around rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise devices that are exploited on demand, used against carefully selected targets, cleaned up after each operation, and continuously refreshed," Black Lotus Labs said.

"This model has enabled Volt Typhoon to conduct exploitation and post-exploitation operations with exceptional operational security while minimizing opportunities for detection, attribution, and disruption."

A defining characteristic of these attacks is the repeated targeting of systems that can open the door to broad visibility, control, and access across large enterprise environments of strategic value to the U.S.

Researcher Reveals How Logic Bugs Alone Cracked Microsoft Edge in $175,000 Pwn2Own WinSwati KhandelwalOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Browser Security

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

A chain of logic flaws, with no memory corruption, can turn a malicious web page into code running on a Windows computer outside Microsoft Edge's sandbox, a security researcher has shown.

Orange Tsai of DEVCORE published the full method on October 28, five months after the chain won $175,000 at the Pwn2Own Berlin contest in May. Microsoft fixed the Edge bugs the day after the contest, so an up-to-date browser is not at risk.

A browser sandbox is the wall that keeps a web page's code inside the browser and off the rest of the computer. Breaking out of it, and then running a program, is what turns a web bug into full control of the machine.

Browser escapes like this almost always rely on memory corruption. This one used none. In his write-up, Tsai describes a chain built solely from logic errors in how Edge and Windows handle ordinary features, and he says the whole exploit is under 100 lines of code.

The result is a universal cross-site scripting (UXSS) primitive: a way to run JavaScript on any website, bypassing the content security policy meant to prevent it.

Because the attack starts from the browser's own process, it can reach sites like google.com that an ordinary web bug cannot touch. Tsai calls this a new attack surface rather than a one-off bug.

This was a competition exploit, not an attack seen in the wild. Tsai demonstrated it on stage at Pwn2Own; there is no evidence it has been used against real users, and the public CVE records list exploitation as none. One step in the chain restarts the browser, which Tsai notes is a convenience for the contest and not needed in a real attack.

The chain begins with an Edge feature for business sign-ins called a conditional access navigation throttle. Tsai found that triggering it lets the browser's own process start a new navigation that is not tied to the page that asked for it, so Edge attaches it to whichever tab is open. That mismatch is the first bug, and it produces the UXSS.

Making it run without a click took four more weaknesses. Edge checked that the request came from a trusted Microsoft site, but Tsai bypassed the check by opening the request from a second window. Edge's popup blocker should have stopped that window, but Edge carried a hardcoded list of allowed addresses, and one of them opened the popup.

The attack also required the victim to be already signed in, which the Edge auto-sign-in feature provides on its own when the user visits a Microsoft site. Lastly, the chain reads the victim's email address from a Microsoft site, assets.msn.com, which returned it to any website due to a misconfigured cross-origin setting.

Running JavaScript everywhere is still not in control of the computer. To escape the sandbox, Tsai used Edge's reading mode, Immersive Reader, which runs under a custom read:// address that Microsoft left off the list of pages barred from running scripts.

From there, the chain called an internal Edge function meant to zip up diagnostic logs and abused it to write a file with an attacker-chosen name and content anywhere on disk.

That file write is turned into code execution in two steps. The chain overwrites a configuration file that controls which websites may launch which protocol handlers, then restarts Edge so the file is read. It then launches a telnet:// link; because Windows does not ship a telnet program by default, it searches the system path for one and runs an attacker-planted copy from a folder the low-privileged user can write to.

Cyber intrusions targeting the legal sector nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, reflecting the value of legal entities to both eCrime and nation-state adversaries. Legal entities hold privileged communications, corporate transactions, intellectual property, government matters, and financial records that make them valuable targets for threat actors seeking financial gain or long-term strategic intelligence. 
The CrowdStrike 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report analyzes threat activity observed from September 1, 2025 through August 31, 2026. It includes the key themes, trends, and events shaping the legal sector threat landscape, as well as anticipatory assessments and actionable recommendations to help the sector prepare for the continued evolution of modern threats.
The breadth and complexity of threats targeting the legal sector are evident in this analysis. As AI technology advances, adversaries are likely to accelerate the scale and sophistication of their operations, putting greater pressure on defenders. This evolving environment demands continuous intelligence-driven defense to detect and stop threats.  
eCrime Makes Up 82% of Threats to Legal Entities
Financially motivated adversaries accounted for 82% of observed activity against the legal sector. They can profit from attacks on legal entities by deploying ransomware or monetizing stolen data through extortion or resale on criminal markets. Big game hunting adversaries named 455 legal entities on dedicated leak sites, a 39% year-over-year increase. 
CHATTY SPIDER is a dominant threat: Their activity surged 129% in the first eight months of 2026 compared to all of 2024, and law firms made up nearly 90% of their victims during the reporting period. The adversary typically resumes data theft and extortion campaigns following a mid-year hiatus; however, they returned from this break slightly earlier than usual in 2026.
This adversary almost exclusively targeted U.S.-based law firms, a trend highly likely to continue. They manipulate victims by impersonating IT staff to establish remote access sessions and exfiltrate sensitive data within minutes, and they increasingly use trusted enterprise tools to do it.
In November 2025, CHATTY SPIDER hired a Russian national to physically access a U.S.-based law firm. The individual posed as an internal IT employee and was granted access to an onsite workstation, where he enabled the adversary to deploy remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools and attempted to exfiltrate data via cloud storage services. While the individual was detained during a second attempted visit, public reporting indicates CHATTY SPIDER used U.S.-based individuals to conduct several physical intrusions during 2026. 
SNARKY SPIDER, which emerged in October 2025, and CORDIAL SPIDER, which emerged in November 2025, are both significant eCrime threats to the legal sector. Both have targeted legal entities in high-tempo data theft and extortion campaigns. They share nearly identical tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), including vishing calls that impersonate IT personnel and directing employees to single sign-on (SSO)-themed phishing pages. Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what appears to be an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted attack orchestrated by a suspected China-nexus threat actor that has leveraged the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to breach exposed systems.

The activity, which was observed on October 25, 2026, involved an attacker combining PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including three systems in a U.S. government-affiliated environment.

"The affected devices run specific versions of a large vendor's firewall software," cybersecurity firm Dream said. "The attacker then launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration."

The name of the affected vendor was not disclosed, but the Israeli company said it notified the entity. The attack chain essentially brings together two sets of vulnerabilities impacting PHP and the Linux kernel -

PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2) that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution
Fragnesia, a Linux kernel local privilege escalation vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-46300 (CVSS score: 7.8)

"The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell," Dream researchers explained. "It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform."

"The vulnerability targets PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the firewall's appweb management server. The firewall OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack."

The custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain, coupled with CVE-2026-46300, is said to have rooted 25 servers across the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

Artifacts discovered by Dream indicate that the operation started with exploit development in a lab environment before obtaining persistent access to a U.S. government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

"Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a U.S. government-affiliated environment," the company noted.

The links to AI-assisted tooling stem from evidence pointing to the installation of Anthropic's Claude Code in the attack infrastructure, along with the presence of API keys for FOFA and an AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan configured with large language models (LLMs) from DeepSeek and Kimi.

What's more, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across nearly 40 scripts suggest the use of AI to augment the development process. The entire operation, per Dream, unfolds as follows -

Attacker uses FOFA to identify approximately 19,000 internet-facing firewalls with exposed management interfaces worldwide.
A custom version scanner is executed to determine which among those devices are online and what operating system version they are running. About 5,000 devices respond with the version information.
The attacker filters the servers to those located in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and then limits the scope to systems that match newer release branches running PHP 8.0.30. This step yields 240 targets.
The target list is fed as input to an automated batch runner that exploits the PHP2Shell-Fragnesia chain, plants a PHP web shell on a publicly accessible directory on the firewall, verifies root access, and logs the target's hostname and IP to a CSV file. Threat actors are beginning to probe for a newly patched critical vulnerability in Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS), according to threat intelligence firm Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS score: 9.8) , a case of improper authentication in the Oracle Application Object Library of Oracle E-Business Suite. It was patched by Oracle last week as part of its Critical Patch Update.

Security researchers Brandon Peterson, Jimi Sebree, and Noah King of Horizon3.ai have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw to Oracle on July 24, 2026.

"Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, October 27," Defused Cyber said in an X post.

In an advisory for the vulnerability, Horizon3.ai described it as an unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability that could be chained to achieve remote code execution.

"The vulnerability allows an attacker with network access to the affected Thin Client Framework (TCF) servlet to execute SQL as the APPS database user, then run operating system commands as the EBS application account," the cybersecurity company said.

Specifically, an attacker can issue a crafted request to the vulnerable TCF servlet at "/OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer" to run SQL with the privileges of the APPS database user and ultimately enable system command execution with the privileges of the EBS application account.

Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-101767 can permit an attacker to read or modify application data accessible to APPS and execute commands on the application host.

"Depending on the deployment, affected data may include financial, payroll, HR, and procurement records. Operating system access is governed by the permissions of the compromised EBS application account," Horizon3.ai warned.

While internet-facing EBS deployments present the most risk, internal EBS systems can also be exploited if an attacker can reach the vulnerable servlet from a compromised system or another accessible network segment.

Users are advised to update to the latest version as soon as possible. If immediate patching is not an option, the following workarounds can be applied -

Remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, associated with oracle.apps.fnd.tcf.SocketServer, from the EBS URL firewall allowlist.
Restrict access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks.
Monitor the EBS application host and database for signs of compromise.

Horizon3.ai has also shared the below indicators of compromise -

Unauthenticated POST requests to /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer that instantiate the Gantt data-server class (oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer), followed by backend database activity.
SQL reconnaissance shortly after unauthenticated web requests (database version, current user, directory objects).
Unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account spawning /bin/sh via the Concurrent Manager to run OS commands.

Vulnerabilities in EBS are a hot target for attackers. Over the past year, two critical flaws in the same product (CVE-2025-61882 and CVE-2026-46817, CVSS scores: 9.8) have come under active exploitation, with the former leveraged by the Cl0p ransomware and extortion crew.

title: Critical 16-Year-Old UEFI Flaw Can Run Code Before Secure Boot on Network-Booting Servers
text:
Critical 16-Year-Old UEFI Flaw Can Run Code Before Secure Boot on Network-Booting ServersSwati KhandelwalOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

A critical 16-year-old flaw in EDK II, the open-source code that most hardware makers use to build UEFI firmware, can allow an attacker to run code on a machine before its operating system loads, but only while the machine is booting over the network.

UEFI firmware is the software that runs first when a computer is switched on, before the operating system. An attacker who can reach the machine with a crafted network message during such a network boot can hang the boot, or, with work tailored to the exact firmware build, run their own code before Secure Boot and other startup defenses load.

An attacker needs no password and no existing access to the machine, but does need to reach it over the network during the short window when it is booting this way.

Red Hat and SUSE, which both ship the affected code, rated the flaw as one an attacker exploits from an adjacent network position rather than across the open internet.

TianoCore, the project behind EDK II, published an advisory on October 22 and rated the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, 9.5 out of 10. A code fix exists, but no stable release of EDK II contains it yet, and the advisory still lists no patched version, so most users have nothing to install today.

What the Flaw Lets an Attacker Do

The flaw is a buffer overflow in EDK II's network-boot code, known as PXE. During a PXE boot, a machine loads its startup image from the network instead of from a local disk.

As part of this, the PXE driver listens for ICMP error messages and the small status messages that network devices send back, and copies each one into a fixed 504-byte area of memory.

The size checks in that copy are wrong in both the IPv4 and IPv6 versions of the code, so a message longer than 504 bytes spills past the area and overwrites nearby memory with data the attacker chose.

To set this off, an attacker only has to send one crafted error message to the machine's address while it is in the middle of a network boot. No password or existing access to the machine is needed.

The simple result is a crash: the boot hangs, and the machine fails to start. Getting code to run is much harder and far less reliable. The advisory says that an attacker who knows the exact firmware build can plant a "counterfeit event" that causes the firmware to run the attacker's own code, so an exploit has to be built for a specific build.

When code runs, it executes within the firmware, before Secure Boot and other boot-time checks have verified anything. That timing is what makes the flaw serious.

Code planted this way runs only once and does not survive a reboot by itself. That single run is still enough to install other code that does start on every boot.

Who Is Affected

The bug sits in EDK II up to and including edk2-stable202608, the newest stable version, dated August 21. EDK II is the reference code that nearly every UEFI firmware vendor builds on, including the independent BIOS makers AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, as well as Microsoft's hardened fork, Project Mu.

The flawed copy loop has been in the code since a commit added in November 2010, The Hacker News found by tracing the project's history.

PXE network boot is turned on by default in EDK II's standard build. The flaw does not affect home or office users who boot only from a local disk. It applies to organizations whose machines boot over a network, primarily servers and data center equipment.

An unreleased Anthropic AI model found security flaws in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux and chained them into working proof-of-concept exploits, the company said in its latest report.

The exploits were built in the lab after the model was prompted, not seen in any real attack, and Anthropic reported every flaw to the vendor first, so all of them are already patched. One proof of concept opened the Calculator app on a stock Mac running Chrome within seconds of a page loading, with no further clicks.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described five chains in a research post. The strongest claim is not any single bug, but that one model found several separate flaws and combined them into a working exploit, something the company says has until now been the work of a few specialist teams. That capability claim rests on Anthropic's own account.

The patches and the fact that Apple and Google credit Anthropic and its Claude model for specific fixes can be verified with the vendors.

What a reader cannot check is how much of each chain the model built on its own. Anthropic says the work needed only "initial prompting" and "little human involvement," but it does not break down what a person did at each step, and it does not name the model beyond calling it an unreleased, internal research model.

ShinyHunters-Exploited Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day Turns Out to Be Three Chained FlawsSwati KhandelwalOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security

The critical Oracle PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May is not one flaw but three chained together, the researchers who reported it said this week.

Oracle patched all three under a single identifier, CVE-2026-35273, in June. Its root is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches an internal management interface because PeopleSoft trusts its own loopback address by default, opening the door to remote code execution without a login.

The breakdown comes from Bobby Gould of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), whose team reported the flaw to Oracle.

In its analysis, ZDI said it reported three distinct vulnerabilities across two PeopleSoft components, and that it is working with Oracle to assign a separate CVE to each. As of this week, the one June identifier is still the only one on the record.

CVE-2026-35273 affects PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62, carries a CVSS score of 9.8, and lets an unauthenticated attacker take over the server over the network. Oracle released its fix in an out-of-band security alert on June 10. The flaw is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Attackers were already using it before that fix was in place. Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) attribute a campaign to the group it tracks as UNC6240, better known as ShinyHunters, that exploited the flaw between May 27 and June 9, mostly against universities. Because that activity came before Oracle's June 10 advisory, it was a zero-day the whole time.

In a September follow-up, Mandiant reported a renewed, larger wave that spread beyond education to technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transport, and government, affecting dozens of systems worldwide.

ZDI's analysis explains what that single patch actually closed. Two PeopleSoft components are involved, both run as separate web applications. The Integration Gateway (PSIGW) exchanges messages with outside systems. The Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) is an internal admin interface that is supposed to answer only to trusted hosts.

The first flaw is the SSRF in PSIGW. An attacker sends a request to its listening connector and controls both the address it forwards to and the full payload it sends, ZDI said; the handler does no check that the destination is a legitimate target. That alone would be limited, except for what it can reach.

PSEMHUB decides who to trust by checking the requester against a list in a file named allowedhosts.properties. That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list. So an attacker points the SSRF at 127.0.0.1, the request arrives looking like it came from the machine itself, and the trust check passes. The internal interface Oracle meant to wall off is now reachable from outside.

From there, ZDI described two ways to turn that access into code execution. One abuses a PSEMHUB command meant to write log entries: the caller controls both the file contents and the exact path on disk, so an attacker writes a web shell into the application directory and runs commands as the PeopleSoft service account.

The other writes a malicious XML file that PSEMHUB reads using Java's XMLDecoder when the service next starts, thereby running the attacker's code without planting a web shell at all. The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.

The design decision at the center, ZDI said, is that allowing loopback access by default makes the trust check ineffective once the SSRF exists. That matters for defenders who thought a firewall rule had covered them.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added two vulnerabilities impacting Adobe Commerce and Magento, and Google's Brotli decoder library to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.
CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) - An unrestricted upload of a file with dangerous type vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session.

The development comes days after Sansec said it observed attackers leveraging CVE-2026-48356, also known as PolyShell, to breach hundreds of e-commerce stores to inject a malicious loader via a Magento CMS block.

The loader is designed to fetch and execute an attacker-controlled payload, although no next-stage malware has been recovered to date, making it challenging to determine what the exact goals of the campaign are. The activity is assessed to be ongoing since at least July 2025.

As for CVE-2026-111497 (aka Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell), telemetry data from threat intelligence firm Previdian shows that one exploitation attempt has been recorded against its honeypot sensors from a U.S.-based IP address as of October 27, 2026. It's currently not known if these efforts are broad in scope.

"An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory," Rapid7 said. "According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder."

ELLIO also reported on Monday that its sensors "have recorded CVE-2026-111497 exploit traffic in the wild, carrying the public exploit that we confirmed gets a shell on vulnerable builds." The activity originates from "94.154.43[.]7," an IP address geolocated to the Netherlands that has also engaged in exploitation efforts targeting PHP2Shell, two critical flaws in PHP that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution.

"The attacker's payload is a genuine, correctly-structured Node2Shell exploitation attempt for node v24.22.0 – the Brotli stream, staged displacement, pivot pair, and delivery are all correct and identical to the public tooling," ELLIO said. "This is indicative of the RCE being adopted by an operator focused on mass exploitation."

The fact that Brotli is a widely distributed open-source library and adopted by numerous projects has provoked an emergency response, prompting various vendors to release patches or assess if their products are affected by the flaw.

Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 10/28/2026 08:30 AM PDT

Description:

AWS SDK for pandas (awswrangler) is an open-source Python library that integrates pandas with AWS data services such as Amazon Athena, Amazon S3, and AWS Glue. We identified CVE-2026-118029 in the Athena module, where unverified ownership of the default query result location could allow a remote user to read Athena query results and tamper with result sets returned to the caller via a pre-created S3 bucket.

This issue has been addressed in AWS SDK for pandas version 3.16.1, released May 8, 2026. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Verify that the default Athena result bucket in each account and Region is owned by your own account, and set an explicit result location or enforce a workgroup result configuration.

CVE-2026-115415 - Secret masking bypass in the environment tool in Strands Agents Tools

Bulletin ID: 2026-154-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 10/28/2026 12:30 PM PDT

Description:

Strands Agents Tools (strands-agents-tools) is an open-source Python package of pre-built tools for the Strands Agents SDK. The environment tool lets an agent list, read, set, and delete environment variables on the agent host, and masks values that look like secrets by default. We identified CVE-2026-115415, an issue where the environment tool accepted a masking parameter from the large language model (LLM) through its tool schema. A crafted prompt, delivered through content the agent is asked to process, could instruct the model to call the tool with masking turned off. The tool would then return the agent host's environment variables in cleartext, including cloud credentials and API keys, without prompting the operator for consent.

Impacted versions: >= 0.1.0 AND < 0.8.6

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in strands-agents-tools version 0.8.6. Masking is now controlled only by the operator, and the model can no longer disable it. The environment tool is also deprecated as of this release. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. We also recommend rotating any credentials that were present in the environment of agents that loaded the environment tool.

Workarounds:

If you cannot upgrade right away, remove the environment tool from your agents. Avoid running agents with long-lived cloud credentials or API keys in the process environment, and restrict outbound network access from the agent host to trusted endpoints only.

References:

CVE-2026-115415

title: What Your Browser Tells Every Website You Visit (And Why I Finally Checked Mine)
text: Today I opened AmIUnique.org in my browser just to see what it would say. The first line on the screen was:"Yes! You are unique among 5,635,779 fingerprints in our entire dataset."My first reaction was, wait, is that good or bad? I use Brave. I use a VPN. I work in security every day. I thought I had this covered. So I sat down and went through the results line by line. That's why I'm writing this. Most people never look at what their browser is sharing, and once you do, you start to see the internet differently. So what is a browser fingerprint?Every time you open a website, your browser introduces itself. It doesn't ask permission. It just tells the site things like:Your operating system (Windows, Mac, Linux)Your browser and its exact versionYour language and time zoneYour screen sizeThe fonts installed on your machineHow many CPU cores and how much memory you haveWhat your graphics card draws when asked to render a hidden image (this is called canvas and WebGL fingerprinting)On its own, each item is boring. Millions of people run Windows. Millions use 1920x1080 screens. But put 50 of these small details together and you get a combination that is often unique to you. That combination is your fingerprint.The scary part is that it doesn't need cookies. You can clear your cookies, open a private window, and a site can still recognize you from your fingerprint. What I found when I tested my own browserHere is roughly what AmIUnique showed me:OS: Windows, which 44% of their users shareBrowser: Chrome-based (Brave), shared by 48%Language: English, shared by 66%Time zone: UTC+1, shared by 15%Canvas fingerprint: 0.00%. Nobody else matched.Plugins: names like "ufu2EhvX" and "LNGqVpz". That one made me laugh.CPU cores: 29. I don't have 29 cores.That's when it clicked. Those weird values weren't my real machine. Brave was lying for me on purpose. It changes the values each time a site reads them, so I look unique on every visit, but differently each time. A tracker can't link Monday's visit to Tuesday's because the fingerprint keeps changing.The site also showed that no similar fingerprint had been seen in the last 90 days, not even from my own earlier visits. That's exactly what you want.So being "unique" isn't always bad. Unique and stable is bad, because that's trackable. Unique and changing every time is protection. What still gave me awayEven with Brave doing its job, a few things still leaked:IP address. This is the big one. Every site sees it. In my case it was a VPN address, not my home connection, so that one was covered.Time zone. My browser said UTC+1. If my VPN says I'm in the US but my clock says Central Europe, any site that compares the two can see it.Language vs. location. An en-US language with a UTC+1 time zone is a slightly unusual pairing, and unusual means easier to pick out.Fonts. The standard Windows font set shows up clearly.Do Not Track. Ironically, turning it on adds one more small detail about you.None of these are a disaster on their own, but they add up. Why this matters, especially if you do investigationsFor a normal user, this is about privacy and ad tracking. For anyone doing OSINT, threat research or incident response, that's a different level.Think about it. You're investigating a phishing site, a scam shop or a threat actor's forum. You open their page in your normal work browser. What did you just tell them?Your real time zone, which hints at your countryYour company's IP address, unless you're on a VPNYour language settingsA fingerprint they can match the next time you visitIf the person on the other side is paying attention, and good ones do, you might have just told them someone is looking at them and roughly where that someone sits. Some actors block or redirect visitors who look like researchers. Some serve different content. Some just quietly take notes.And this goes both ways. Sometimes you don't want to look hidden. A browser that is too locked down also stands out. If every visitor to a […]

Update: Brotli flaw exposure expands

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

Analysis conducted since the disclosure of CVE-2026-111497 has identified additional affected products, including Palo Alto PAN-OS, Prisma Cloud Application Security Transporter Client, DuckDB, Apache Arrow, ClickHouse, MuPDF, and several other projects that bundle vulnerable Brotli code.

New research shows the vulnerable Google Brotli decoder may be reachable through file-processing workflows, not just web traffic.

Organizations that process untrusted files, inspect Brotli traffic, or automatically decompress external content may face greater exposure than initially understood.

Threat summary
Analysis following the disclosure of CVE-2026-111497 (also referred to as Brotli2Shell, Broccoli2Shell, Node2Shell, and HTTP2Shell) has expanded the list of products affected by the vulnerable Google Brotli decoder and improved understanding of where exploitable attack paths may exist.
Early reporting focused primarily on software ecosystems known to bundle the decoder, including Node.js, .NET, Python, Envoy, Istio, and Bun.
Between October 24 and 27, additional vendor advisories identified affected:

Versions of Palo Alto PAN-OS

Prisma Cloud Application Security Transporter Client

PowerShell 7.4, 7.5, and 7.6

Visual Studio 2019, 2022, and 2026

The Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 Brotli package

Investigations also identified vulnerable bundled Brotli implementations in projects including ClickHouse, DuckDB, Apache Arrow, MuPDF, NanaZip, GraalJS, and libjxl.
JPEG XL and FFmpeg
One of the most significant findings involves libjxl, the reference implementation of the JPEG XL image format, which uses Brotli to decompress metadata embedded in JPEG XL files.
Research published on October 25 demonstrated that a specially crafted JPEG XL image could reach the vulnerable Brotli decoder when processed by an affected FFmpeg deployment. Researchers demonstrated memory corruption and instruction-pointer control within FFmpeg, showing that the vulnerability can be reached through file-processing workflows rather than network traffic alone. This expands potential exposure beyond web applications to any system that processes untrusted JPEG XL content.
Other product impacts
The same research showed a remote crash in ClickHouse from a single malicious request, a crash in the .NET runtime, and an infinite loop in Apache Arrow that results in denial of service.
Infrastructure impacts
Palo Alto PAN-OS is affected when both TLS decryption and Brotli inspection are enabled. Brotli inspection is disabled by default and is available beginning with PAN-OS 11.2.4.
Affected releases include vulnerable 11.2.4 and later 11.2 builds, along with affected 12.1 and 12.2 releases prior to available hotfixes.
PAN-OS 11.1, 10.2, Panorama, and the management interface are outside the scope of the issue. Envoy and Istio deployments are affected only when Brotli decompression has been explicitly configured.
Exploitation reporting
On October 26, a single threat intelligence source reported observing an exploitation attempt targeting Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64 systems.
Independent confirmation of the reported activity has not been published.
Analysis
Node.js remains the most exposed software ecosystem identified to date. Public proof-of-concept code, researcher demonstrations, and the only publicly reported exploitation attempt have all focused on Node.js deployments. Researchers demonstrated code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 under specific conditions, and subsequent reporting identified attack paths involving both Brotli-compressed request bodies and applications that retrieve Brotli-compressed content from external sources.

It’s not often acknowledged, but cyber security owes a lot to volunteers. People who are dedicated enough to give up their time to help others through building open source tools, being available as mentors, or running training.
Alwell Mulsid is head of Cyber Incident Response Section at CERT-PH in the Philippines - a brand new full member of FIRST - and on weekends he runs the Philippine Cybersecurity Union of IT and Computer Science Professionals (PH Cyber Units for short). These are technically focused training sessions for cyber security professionals from government and private sector organizations.
The reason why is that the Philippines' frontline cybersecurity experts have a scheduling problem. The people who most need advanced technical skills can rarely get approval to leave their desks for training. Weekdays belong to operations. Weekends belong to everything else.
Alwell saw that gap and decided to fill it with a volunteer-run, non-profit advocacy group that trains people on their own time for free.
The model is deliberately old-school with face-to-face interactions and a BYOD set-up. While webinars are cheap and scalable, Mulsid found they often fall short on complex subjects like forensics, where the learning happens “in the doing, not in the watching”.
What the PH Cyber Unit covers isn't set from a standard curriculum. Topics come directly from what natCSIRT responders encounter in the field, so participants practice on the problems they'll actually meet. The current offering is a three-module laddered series on incident response and forensics, building from fundamentals toward advanced practice.
Logistics get the same pragmatic treatment. Materials go out in advance, so nobody is stuck downloading large files over unreliable venue wi-fi. Governance is equally grounded. The PH Cyber Units is registered as a non-profit advocacy group with a board of directors drawn from both government and private-sector volunteers.
The last hurdle is venue. It’s tough finding a good spot that can accommodate a room full of cybersecurity people who need power and internet access. Let alone finding one that is accessible on a weekend, which rules out a lot of government buildings, and doesn’t charge hotel conference rates.
PH Cyber Units found the perfect solution: a shopping mall. Malls are accessible by public transport, open on weekends, large enough to absorb serious demand, and those attending the courses can bring their families to shop or watch movies. Registration has now reached as high as 300 applicants for a single session.
The group is Manila-based but has already run trainings in other regions. Alwell’s goal is to create volunteer-led units across the provinces outside the capital. The idea is local people training local people, rather than everyone depending on a single travelling team of outside consultants, even if “outside” is just another part of the country.
As part of this, Alwell stressed to me the importance of boosting women in cybersecurity. Women are very underrepresented in cyber security and even less so in training. So, women-led training for women makes a lot of sense.
A dedicated subunit of PH Cyber does exactly that. It's a small structural choice with an outsized effect. And it is having an effect, changing the perception of who a cyber security expert is.
The community doubles as a networking hub, and the results are tangible: attendees have gone on to land professional cybersecurity roles. For a country short on skilled defenders, that pipeline matters far more than any individual session.

Authors

João Victor

Background
Network-connected surveillance cameras are now widespread in both home and enterprise environments, so securing them is essential to safeguarding physical spaces and sensitive assets. As these devices continue to gain new features and network connectivity capabilities, vulnerabilities in their implementation can have significant security implications.
During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems. The flaw resides in a firmware update endpoint that is accessible without authentication and allows anyone with access to the local Wi-Fi network to knock cameras offline. A single request disrupts the camera for only about a minute, but sending periodic requests keeps the device offline indefinitely. We reported the issue to Intelbras, monitored the remediation process, validated the fix in the new firmware, and will now demonstrate the exploitation procedure step-by-step.
Following our notification, Intelbras patched the vulnerability and released updated firmware (R.260804) along with update instructions. A candidate ID of CAN-2026-2035970 has been assigned by MITRE following submission, pending the final CVE assignment. Additionally, the Intelbras team recently informed us that MITRE has classified the vulnerability as Medium, assigning it a score of 5.1 under the CVSS 4.0 framework. The issue discussed in this article is no longer present in the latest firmware version.
Firmware
Intelbras provides firmware files on its official website. While users can manually install these updates via an SD card, the cameras also natively support firmware upgrades over the local network via their web interface and mobile app. We obtained the firmware version v240927 for the iM3B-C (IM3 C) camera, which was the latest available version at the time of our research. According to Intelbras, the same firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Below, we can view the firmware version and the camera model used as an example.

To provide context, we will explain how the camera’s authentication mechanism works and why it is relevant to accessing the camera’s endpoints. The main firmware component is an ARM binary named sonia, responsible for controlling the kernel drivers used by the camera hardware, authentication, and livestream recording, among other things.
How authentication works
The global.login RPC method handles authentication at the /RPC2_Login endpoint. First, the client, such as the mobile app or a custom script, sends the username and an empty password. The camera responds with an authentication challenge (a set of values to verify the password without transmitting it). This response returns a temporary session, the encryption type in the encryption field, a random value, and a realm (authentication scope). At this stage, a false response is normal and does not indicate a failed login, as the authentication process is not yet complete.
Next, the client calculates the response password from the authentication challenge. It first generates an MD5 (username:realm:original_password) hash as the base. It then calculates a second MD5 (username:random:first_md5) hash,  where first_md5 is the result of the previous step. To complete the authentication, the client sends this final result back to /RPC2_Login in a second global.login call, passing the username, calculated password, and temporary session ID.
If the login is accepted, the camera returns true and a new, authenticated session. This session must be used for all subsequent RPC calls, including the camera’s other endpoints, for example, the one that reboots the device or those that expose sensitive information.

CVE-2026-97631: A 16-year-old UEFI flaw (CVSS score of 9.5/10) enables pre-OS code execution. Exposed servers need firmware patches and checks.

A critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97631 (CVSS score of 9.5), in the firmware that boots most of the world’s servers is now public, and the patch details came out months early.

The bug affects TianoCore EDK II, an open-source project used by hardware manufacturers and cloud providers to build UEFI firmware. UEFI is the software that starts a computer before the operating system loads. EDK II is widely used across the industry, including by major UEFI vendors such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix. Even Microsoft’s more secure version, Project Mu, used the vulnerable component.

“EDK2 contains a vulnerability in BIOS where a user may cause “Out-of-bounds Write”, Classic Buffer Overflow, and “Incorrect Calculation of Buffer Size” by remote access. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to arbitrary code execution. It could also impact Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.” reads the advisory.

The flaw can corrupt memory in a component that handles ICMP messages, which devices use to report network errors. Attackers could exploit it to run code before the operating system starts and before security protections such as Secure Boot are fully active. Secure Boot checks that the software loaded during startup can be trusted, while the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) supports security functions such as hardware-based trust. Although the attacker’s code does not remain active after execution, it could help attackers install other malicious components that run early in the boot process.

title: CVE-2026-115881: Critical GoAhead TLS Flaw Allows Revoked Client Certificates
text:
A critical vulnerability in the GoAhead embedded web server can allow revoked client certificates to remain valid during mutual TLS authentication, potentially giving previously trusted identities continued access to protected devices and services.

Tracked as CVE-2026-115881, the flaw carries a vendor-assigned CVSS score of 9.1 and affects GoAhead versions 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 when the software uses its OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend with certificate revocation lists configured. The issue was fixed in GoAhead 6.1.1.

GoAhead is an embedded web server commonly integrated into routers, printers, gateways, industrial systems, and other network-connected products. However, the vulnerability does not affect every GoAhead installation. Exploitation requires a specific mutual TLS configuration, and the affected population of commercial devices has not been established.

The vulnerability stems from improper certificate revocation validation. GoAhead successfully loads a configured Certificate Revocation List (CRL) into OpenSSL’s certificate store, but fails to activate the OpenSSL flag required to enforce CRL checking. Consequently, a certificate explicitly marked as revoked can still complete authentication.

For CVE-2026-115881 detection, security teams should combine software inventory, TLS backend identification, certificate telemetry, and monitoring of mutual TLS authentication. Because an affected server treats the revoked certificate as valid, exploitation may not generate an obvious authentication failure or traditional exploit signature.

SOC Prime users can strengthen coverage for exploitation attempts and suspicious post-authentication behavior by correlating identity, network, application, and endpoint telemetry across their security stack.

Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-115881, defenders should first identify vulnerable GoAhead deployments and then monitor for authentication performed with certificates that should already have been revoked.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-115881 analysis

The vulnerability exists in the way GoAhead integrates Certificate Revocation List validation with its OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend.

In mutual TLS, both sides authenticate using digital certificates. Organizations can revoke a client certificate when a device is retired, an employee loses access, a private key is compromised, or the associated identity should otherwise no longer be trusted.

A CRL provides the server with a list of certificates that must be rejected.

Researchers at FoxIO found that GoAhead correctly loads the configured CRL using OpenSSL, but fails to enable the X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK verification flag. Loading a CRL into the certificate store alone does not cause OpenSSL to check certificate revocation status.

As a result, certificate verification can complete successfully even when the client certificate appears on the configured revocation list.

FoxIO reproduced the issue using GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2. During testing, a revoked client certificate signed by a trusted CA successfully completed an mTLS handshake even when issuer verification was enabled. The server generated no startup warning indicating that revocation checking was ineffective.

This silent failure is particularly significant because administrators may reasonably assume that configuring a CRL means revoked certificates will be rejected.

The details for CVE-2026-115881 show that exploitation requires several conditions to be present:

GoAhead must use the OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend.

The deployment must require client certificates.

A trusted CA bundle must be configured.

Certificate issuer verification must be enabled for the clearest security impact.

A CRL must be configured.

The attacker must possess a certificate issued by the trusted authority that has subsequently been revoked.

text:
A leak website was published Wednesday, showcasing internal data on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors after it was obtained by hackers who claimed to have breached an identity service used by the agency.

The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and the hacker maia arson crimew got the data from a hacktivist outfit known as the Department of Peace.

”The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in [its] simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs,” said Emma Best, founder of DDoSecrets.

CyberScoop was able to verify numerous current Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency employees are listed in the data, along with some former leadership members who left the agency years ago.

The data goes back years, with various group names listed in the database making reference to COVID-19 planning and internal summits in 2023.

The hacktivists said the breach was a response to the promise of stepped-up operations from Immigrations and Customs Enforcement by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

”On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ’turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” said a spokesperson for the Department of Peace.

The spokesperson said they obtained the database from an Okta single sign-on service used at DHS. Okta said it was aware of the report.

“Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” an Okta spokesperson said.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

”This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” said crimew, a Swiss hacker and journalist who has been indicted in the United States over past leaks and who created a search tool for the DHS data. “It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security’s organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE.”

One researcher said the leak could prove valuable for Freedom of Information Act requests.

“Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent.”

DHS has suffered notable breaches before, dating back to a 2014 breach that may have exposed the data of 390,000 then-current and former Homeland Security Department employees, job applicants and contractors. In 2018, DHS notified nearly 250,000 people of a breach at the department.

Earlier this year, Security firm GitGuardian said it discovered a public GitHub repository that exposed credentials for privileged AWS GovCloud accounts and internal CISA systems dating back to November 2025.

Greg Otto contributed to this story.

When enterprises need to make decisions on open-ended matters, they usually turn to human experts for the final call. But research from Anthropic suggests human experts often rely on AI agents' recommendations, even when the agent has a distinct point of view.See Also: Live Webinar | Go From Awareness to Action in the Post-Quantum Era

Anthropic found that human analysts went with the option their AI agents favored 86% of the time. Of the 50 analysts who participated in an experiment set up by the frontier AI lab, 77%, repeated the agents' reasoning, although only a small percentage credited the agent.

"As AI takes over more of the hands-on work, decisions like these are increasingly where human judgment and values will affect the result. If experts defer to agents without realizing it, the agents' preferences - which could be arbitrary or misaligned - could shape important decisions about policy proposals or research directions without anyone having chosen those preferences," Anthropic said in a blog post.

The company added that these findings are "particularly important for research into keeping AI safe" because human review has become a common check against agentic misbehavior. But it only works if humans make their own judgments.

Anthropic asked 61 professional analysts to run a realistic statistical analysis using Claude Code to advise a farming cooperative. Of these analysts, 11 opted not to use the agents. The others were asked to help a fictional organization, the Greenfields Farming Cooperative, decide whether to keep a program that advises on improving crop yields.

Anthropic gave the analysts and agents one hard rule: the program will expand only if productivity improves by 3% to 4%t. Anthropic also carved out four decisions for the experts to make. The analysts needed to figure out the outcome and whether they should measure productivity as crop yield or yield per unit of operating cost, and whether to compare how farm yields changed since joining the program over other farms or compare yields directly. They also had to decide whether to either measure the effect only in enrolled farms or throughout the collective - and if they should count each farm equally or weigh more toward larger producers.

Anthropic made each agent lean towards certain decisions, which they decided via coin flip and encoded in hidden instructions. The agents were told to hold each point of view and make the strongest case for it, but if the evidence didn't hold up against their lean, they were told not to misrepresent information.

The company said that on each of the four decisions analysts had to make, most experts matched their agents' recommendations, most often for the outcome measure. For the final decision, whether to close or expand the advisory program, the agent's preferences mattered less, but Anthropic said experts already believed the agents' analysis, which shaped how they viewed the final recommendation. Some analysts also changed their opinion when their agent disagreed.

Despite the findings, Anthropic said the experimental results are "a simple cautionary tale against working with AI." Analysts who used an agent "finished the task faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who chose to work without it, although the latter group was small and less experienced, so we are wary of reading too much into it."

Image: Shutterstock/ISMG
Wine fraud has had a bottle problem for ages: Replace the contents, reuse an authentic bottle, reproduce the label, misrepresent the region. Though methods have become more sophisticated, the deception is familiar. What is changing is the infrastructure on which authenticity depends. Wine provenance is becoming digital.See Also: 79% of SOCs Use AI. Only 36% Have It in Their Workflows.
Export records, label registries and authentication platforms now sit between the bottle and the claim that buyers are asked to trust. That creates a cybersecurity question the wine sector is now grappling with: What happens when the bottle survives inspection but the authenticating data can't be trusted?
Wine scams should no longer be seen as only counterfeiting, a fraud scheme or intellectual-property infringement. As authentication moves into digital supply chains, the integrity of provenance data becomes part of the security boundary.
Wine Fraud Is Harder to Measure Than Headlines Say
Widely repeated global estimates claim that one in five bottles is counterfeit, and that fraud costs the industry tens of billions of dollars a year. Recorded Future examined the issue in 2022 and concluded that measuring wine fraud is inherently difficult because incidents frequently remain undetected or unreported. It identified the 20% figure as one commonly cited estimate rather than an established measure of global prevalence.
The absence of a reliable global number doesn't make the problem insignificant. Recorded Future identified more than 93 million bottles connected with publicly reported counterfeit-wine cases between January 2020 and June 2022. Fewer than 5,000 of those were confirmed luxury wines.
That challenges the assumption that wine fraud is exclusively a problem for collectors buying a rare Burgundy at auction, since it can operate at an industrial scale. In October 2024, Europol backed a French, Italian and Swiss investigation into a criminal network counterfeiting French Protected Designation of Origin wines. The fake red wine was produced in Italy and distributed through legitimate commercial channels, with some bottles priced at up to 15,000 euros, or around $16,700. Authorities arrested six people and seized wine, cash and other assets in 14 searches.
But a fraudulent product need not travel through an entirely fraudulent supply chain. Once it enters legitimate channels, trust in the product increasingly depends on the records traveling with it.
Provenance Is Becoming a Data Problem
A bottle of wine can simultaneously claim a particular producer, vintage, grape variety, geographical indication, country of origin and production method.
These aren't just marketing claims. They create economic value. A geographical indication can make similar agricultural output premium, vintage influences price and producer identity can change value by orders of magnitude.
The valuable asset, therefore, isn't just the wine but also its relationship with the information describing it. If authentication depends on digital records, their integrity becomes part of product integrity.
Australia Treats Data as Part of Wine Authenticity
Wine Australia operates the Export Label Image Search System, or ELISS, alongside its Wine Australia Licensing and Approval System.
Australian exporters of packaged wine must upload label images before gaining export approval. ELISS can then make these labels searchable, so importers, distributors, retailers and consumers can check whether a label matches wine legitimately exported from Australia. The system was introduced to curb fraud and brand infringement.

Image: Shutterstock

Damage to an undersea cable could severely disrupt internet routes between the United States and Taiwan, Japan or the Philippines and force traffic onto slower detours, according to a new report.See Also: Prioritize Preparation, Basics and Transparency, Experts Urge IRISSCON Attendees

Researchers at the China Strategic Risks Institute published a recent report for the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission warning that Beijing is building the means to sabotage trans-Pacific cables without tipping into open conflict. The commission released the report in September after a string of cable incidents around Taiwan that included a Chinese work barge suspected of damaging a line to the Matsu Islands in March.

The report's vulnerability index scores cables higher if they land in Taiwan or cross waters Beijing claims. Shallow, crowded shipping lanes can add risk too, since a dragged anchor there can pass for an accident.

Four of the 10 highest-scoring cables are still under construction, including Google's TPU and Meta's ORCA. The authors of the report said Chinese-free ownership leaves Beijing with little reason to spare them in the event of a targeted attack.

Losing any one of three of the four direct U.S.-Taiwan cables could leave more peak traffic than the remaining active capacity can carry, researchers found. The Philippines faces the same risk with two of its three direct links to Guam, which is tied to the U.S. mainland by only two direct cables and could be left with almost no margin if either failed - even with every spare fiber pair switched on.

A geopolitical conflict over Taiwan that severed all four cables running directly between the U.S. and Taiwan could leave the broader trans-Pacific network with as little as 2% spare capacity at peak demand (see: China Could Coerce Taiwan by Hacking Comms, Think Tank Warns).
Losing only two cables, JUNO between Japan and the U.S. and the Pacific Light Cable Network, could push peak demand as much as 70% past the capacity operators have switched on.

If trans-Pacific routes were swamped, traffic between Taiwan and the U.S. could detour through the Indian Ocean and across the Atlantic, adding more than 900 milliseconds to each round trip, the report estimates. A lag of 100 milliseconds is enough to trigger timeouts at payment processors, but operators could ease the crunch by lighting unused fiber.

The report also identifies dual-use tools that could reach cables in deep water once considered out of range, including a 4,000-meter-class cutting device from a research center linked to China's state shipbuilder. China also plans to deploy a crewed seabed station around 2030 that the authors said could support sustained operations against cables.

Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chair, said in a statement released with the report that Washington has framed cable security as a capacity issue, but "in reality, it is a warfighting problem."

The report urges Congress to make acoustic sensors a licensing condition for new cables in high-risk areas, put the Department of Homeland Security or another agency in charge of subsea cable security and help fund at least five new repair ships for the region by 2040. Only 62 cable ships operate worldwide, and repairs in the Asia-Pacific already average about 30 days.

It also calls for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency or another body to work with sectors such as financial clearing and health care on outage playbooks that set which data flows get priority. The vulnerability class is PHP Object Injection (CWE-502) combined with a Missing Authorization check (CWE-862). In WordPress, AJAX actions are registered via hooks such as wp_ajax_<action> and wp_ajax_nopriv_<action>. The NVD description states that the plugin does not perform a capability check on a specific AJAX action and then deserializes stored data that an attacker can control. Because the action lacks a capability check, any authenticated user—including a subscriber, which is the lowest-privilege role—can reach it. The action retrieves stored data and passes it to PHP's unserialize() function (or an equivalent deserialization routine). If an attacker can control the serialized string (likely through a separate stored data field that the subscriber can write to), they can supply a crafted serialized payload containing arbitrary PHP objects. When unserialize() processes this payload, it instantiates objects and triggers magic methods such as __wakeup(), __destruct(), or __toString(). If any installed plugin or theme contains a vulnerable gadget chain, this leads to arbitrary code execution or other severe impacts.
The attack surface is the WordPress AJAX API endpoint (/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php), which is publicly accessible. The vulnerable action name is not disclosed in the available data, so no specific parameter names or file paths can be confirmed. This is not sustainable

October 27th, 2026

What a week,
huh? High fives all around—October is
"Cybersecurity Awareness Month", and I think we've all
done a stellar job. If both the New
York Times and NPR
report on one of the at least four or five concurrent
fires I'm fighting, then I think we can say that
yeah, people are aware of cybersecurity. Mission
accomplished, so... could we maybe turn it down a bit?

The current situation is not sustainable: 0-days are
dropping left and right, pre-notifications and
embargoes are broken
for marketing purposes, AI companies compete first
on who commits the most crimes and then pretend to
sell you protection in the form of a DoS on the Open
Source community. "Nice project you got there. Be
a shame if somebody dropped an 0-day on
it."1

Companies are not staffed for this, and no matter what
the industry wants to tell you, you can't AI your way
out of this. Vulnerability discovery has
fundamentally changed, disclosure processes are effectively broken, and patch management
has been a losing proposition for years now. Severe
vulnerabilities are identified and disclosed at a pace
that defenders are unable to keep up with.

This is because it still takes significant resources
to accurately assess the feasibility of a given
vulnerability within your environment; it takes time
to discover your attack surface relevant to the given
attack vector, and it takes even more time to deploy a
fix. As I've said
before, development of the fix is not the
bottleneck. Let me illustrate with examples from the
last couple of days:

"PwnEscape" (CVE-2026-99999)

Initially disclosed as a "KVM escape", this
vulnerability also applies to other
virtualization as well as containers, although that
angle hasn't really gotten much attention. You now
need to assess which possible mitigations might be in
place across your fleet of systems, then determine
whether you can livepatch
your kernels with the custom patches you pull from
upstream or if you want to wait for your upstream OS
provider to deliver a new kernel2 and then all you
have to do is reboot a few thousand systems.

How does AI help you here? Maybe you spend a few
thousand dollars on tokens to use the most advanced
cyber cyber models to develop your own exploit, but in
the end, that doesn't really tell you anything you
didn't already know, and your defensive position and
tasks at hand remain the same.

eMudhra compromise

This one's fun, isn't it? Sure, browsers were all set
quickly, but guess what, there's a few other
things that might use TLS in your environment.
Like... everything. So again, having the
fix is not the bottleneck. Waiting for upstream
packages to release an update only blocks you if you
actually know that you need to pull in that update.

say it, SBOMs? That's really nice. Do show me where
that lists the various vendored
or hard-coded CA trust bundles. Yeah, I didn't

classical, a-human-going-"huh"
