title: AMI publicly proposed a fix for CVE-2026-97631 before the planned coordinated disclosure, Ars reports. TianoCore says an attacker able to reach a vulnerable EDK II device during PXE boot can execute code before the OS loads; its advisory lists no patched version. Check with your firmware vendor and consider disabling network boot if possible.https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/10/code-execution-flaw-in-uefi-firmware-threatens-most-servers-on-planet-earth/#UEFI #Firmware #InfoSec #Cybersecurity
text:
Text
settings

Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.
The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.
The cat has left the bag
The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.
With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”
CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.
As the official advisory puts it:
During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode.IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect […]

Claim Summary
The ransomware group known as Akira has purportedly listed Trulife, an international healthcare and consumer products manufacturer, on its dark web leak site. According to the threat actor, the alleged attack occurred on October 28, 2026. The group claims to have exfiltrated 68GB of corporate data and states it “will upload” the material “soon,” suggesting the publication has not yet occurred at the time of this report.
Trulife is described in the actor’s own post as a company with over 60 years of experience developing and manufacturing specialized healthcare and consumer products, including breastcare solutions, orthotics, lower limb prosthetics, walking aids, and pressure care products. This is an unverified claim and should be treated with skepticism until independently confirmed.
Threat Actor Profile
akira is a ransomware operation that has been active since approximately 2023 and is widely associated with double extortion tactics - encrypting victim systems while also exfiltrating data to pressure payment. The group is generally assessed to be a financially motivated cybercriminal enterprise rather than an ideologically driven actor.
Public reporting has linked Akira to exploitation of internet-facing VPN appliances and edge devices, including known vulnerabilities in enterprise remote access products, as an initial access vector. The group is also reported to use commodity tooling and living-off-the-land techniques, though specific tooling for this alleged incident has not been disclosed. No public research references were provided for this claim, and the group’s total victim count remains unknown in the supplied data.
Akira has a mixed but notable track record. It has claimed numerous victims across healthcare, manufacturing, and professional services, which lends some surface plausibility to a healthcare-sector claim. However, like most ransomware brands, it routinely inflates data volumes and sensitivity to increase pressure on victims. Credibility for any single claim should be assessed as moderate at best until corroborated.
Alleged Data Exposure
According to the threat actor, the purported 68GB dataset includes:

Detailed employee information, allegedly including passport scans, driver’s licenses, medical certificates, and birth certificates
Contracts and agreements
Confidential files, allegedly covering employee violations and terminations
Financial records
Non-disclosure agreements

These are the actor’s claims only. No data samples, files, or evidence have been independently reviewed for this report. The described categories are typical of what ransomware groups assert to maximize leverage, and the inclusion of identity documents is a common pressure tactic. Yazoul Security does not reproduce, link to, or provide access to any allegedly leaked material.
Potential Impact
If the claim is accurate, the exposure of identity documents and HR records could create significant regulatory, privacy, and reputational risk for a healthcare-adjacent manufacturer. Healthcare data carries heightened sensitivity under many privacy regimes, and employee identity documents could enable fraud or social engineering. Supply chain partners and customers may also face downstream risk. None of this is confirmed.
What to Watch For

Independent confirmation from Trulife or its representatives
Regulatory notifications or breach disclosures in relevant jurisdictions
Appearance of the claimed data on the leak site or elsewhere
Follow-on phishing or fraud referencing the alleged breach

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization," said Phillip Wylie, chief security evangelist at Suzu Labs.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service and the October outage
GMO Internet’s Onamae.com virtual desktop service — delivered via a network the firm says contains tens of thousands of servers and noted in the company’s advisory as popular with foreign‑exchange traders — was suspended on October 21. The company said it discovered the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments,” prompting the shutdown of the service.

Scale of impact and the ransom demand
A security alert from the company said as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. The alert also warned that some information may have been accessed. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions, though the firm’s update focused on the server‑side intrusion and its investigation.
On October 21 an extortion email demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen (reported as $50.7m). According to the company statement, GMO Internet refused to pay the ransom. The attackers then notified the firm they would deploy ransomware on October 27 at 12pm.

Facing a stated October 27 deadline, GMO Internet advised customers to run a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power. The firm has been asking customers to ship their PCs so its security team can perform on‑device analysis.
GMO Internet reported that “As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed.” It added that “the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

What this means for foreign‑exchange traders, security teams, and customers

Foreign‑exchange traders: Onamae.com’s popularity with this group and reports of possible unauthorized trading activity put account integrity and transaction history at the center of immediate concern; traders will be watching forensic results tied to server‑side compromises and any evidence that credentials or session tokens were exfiltrated.
Security teams and incident responders: The case underscores two stress points Wylie highlighted — preventing the initial compromise and limiting what attackers can do after gaining access. The firm’s insistence on device collection for hands‑on analysis reflects a priority on root‑cause forensic work when remote containment is uncertain.
Customers and endpoint owners: The firm’s guidance — full virus scan, backups, disconnecting and powering down PCs — was immediate and prescriptive. Customers who ship devices to GMO will be relying on the firm’s stated forensic timeline and the promise that additional arriving devices will be analyzed promptly.

Japan Inc under fire: a broader pattern
GMO’s incident is the latest in a string of security incidents affecting Japanese companies this year. Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data

Kate Park

6:32 AM PDT · October 27, 2026

Japanese internet company GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders.

The IT and internet services giant said on its blog that it believes the attacker has published information allegedly linked to customers and its business. However, the contents are still being verified and the full extent of the incident remains unclear.

GMO Internet has since advised customers to reset their passwords, amid receiving reports of “unauthorized operations” performed on customer trading accounts. The company said 27,000 servers may be affected by the breach.

A spokesperson for GMO Internet did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

The incident comes about a week after the Japanese firm’s cybersecurity unit separately reported finding evidence that a Chinese AI-enabled penetration testing tool called Artex had been used in hacks targeting companies across Japan. However, the company said it has not publicly established a connection between Artex and the breach of Onamae.

The Artex tool was also used to hack financial institutions in South Korea in September, according to a report by CrowdStrike earlier this month. The attacks largely relied on exploiting weak security controls, such as a lack of multi-factor authentication. Artex’s Chinese developer has since stopped public updates and made the AI security tool closed-source after it was linked to cyberattacks targeting banks, per Reuters.

A spokesperson at Japan’s Financial Service Agency (FSA) told TechCrunch that it issued guidance in May urging financial institutions to prepare for a rise in cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

The regulator called for stronger basic defenses, including “vulnerability management, defense-in-depth and incident preparedness,” while encouraging firms to use AI and other security tools, the spokesperson added.

Here’s the timeline of the Onamae breach.

October 21: GMO Internet shut down its Onamae Desktop Cloud service after discovering unauthorized access had occurred to its systems without permission. The IT firm also received an email from hackers demanding about 8 billion yen (~$50 million).

October 22: The Japanese company reported the incident to Japanese police and shared another public update.

October 24: GMO Internet said it would offer customers compensation and alternative service while seeking help from government agencies.

October 25-26: The company began collecting devices from customers to detect malware and better understand the damage.

October 27: The Japanese IT firm said a suspected attacker had posted information that appeared to be linked to the company and its customers. GMO said it was still checking whether the information was genuine.

The race between patches and probes

TP

The Perimeter Desk
The Mailbag

2026-10-28

# The race between patches and probes

It's Wednesday afternoon. Most of the weekly noise has settled now. We're looking at just under 500 data breach reports and 111 exploits in the wild. The volume is high, but you rarely find the signal until someone asks a real question.

My inbox was packed this morning with people trying to figure out what these numbers actually mean, and I picked three questions that show why seeing a headline isn't the same thing as understanding a risk.

**Marcus from Chicago: "We use Oracle E-Business Suite. The patch for CVE-2026-101767 is out, but we can't reboot the production environment until the weekend. How worried should I be that attackers are already probing it?"**

You should be concerned, Marcus, but not panicked. To understand why, you need to understand binary diffing.

A security patch from Oracle is basically a repair kit. But there's a catch. By releasing it, they give out a map to the hole they just plugged. Attackers take the old software version and the new one and put them through a differencing tool. It's like spotting the difference between two almost identical photos. They can find the exact lines of code that changed, and if the patch fixes a buffer overflow in one function, the attacker now knows exactly where that function is and how it works.

Those probes you see? That is just the sound of attackers testing their new exploits on live targets to check if the patch was actually installed. It sounds backward, but the window of vulnerability might actually grow the moment a patch comes out because building the exploit becomes so much easier.

Look at the timing. CVE-2026-101767 is being probed just days after it was disclosed. This isn't some fluke. It is a workflow. Your maintenance window is now a race against someone who has the actual blueprint for your vulnerability.

Some people will argue that Web Application Firewalls and virtual patching can catch these probes before they hit the server. Sure, that is true. But it is a shield, not a cure, and a WAF blocks known payloads, but it cannot fix a memory corruption flaw deep inside your ERP.

The fallout for Oracle EBS users is where things get really ugly, and these systems run payroll and supply chain logistics. If they are hit, you don't just lose some data, and you stop the flow of goods and stop paying your staff. Imagine a major logistics hub waiting until Saturday to patch, and their clients and those clients' customers will feel that ripple by Monday morning.

**Sarah from London: "The news says Moldova's government was hit and 750,000 citizens' records are gone. The reports mention 'foreign involvement.' Can we actually be sure who did this?"**

In a word: no.

I don't trust the attribution of the Moldova attack. I have low confidence in it. There are reports about "foreign involvement," but fingerprints are cheap and easy to fake these days. Attackers often use infrastructure or tools from other groups just to trick people; what would change my mind? To reach a moderate level of confidence, I'd need to see non-public telemetry, and specifically, I want to see command-and-control traffic that overlaps with known state-sponsored targets without following a public pattern.

I distrust fast attribution. It is often used as a political tool rather than a technical conclusion.

This situation rhymes with the NotPetya campaign of 2017. That attack also targeted government infrastructure and caused massive disruption. The parallel lies in the goal: these aren't typical thefts for profit; they are designed to degrade the functionality of a state. However, where the parallel breaks down is in the intent. NotPetya was essentially a wiper disguised as ransomware. The Moldova event appears more focused on data exfiltration and targeted disruption of specific government systems.

Until we see the actual samples of the malware used […]

2.58 Million Records Gone. The Response Was Minimalist.

TP

Post-Mortem

2026-10-28

# 2.58 Million Records Gone. The Response Was Minimalist.

About 2.58 million users from So-net and Plala just had their data leaked. That's the sort of number that gets a lead engineer woken up at 3am (and for good reason); this isn't some minor corporate headache. It's a full blown identity crisis for a huge chunk of the Japanese internet.

The breach shows exactly what happens when there is a gap between detection and disclosure. Sony is sticking to the script. They're investigating, they regret the inconvenience, and they're talking to the authorities. Notice what they don't say? No mention of dwell time. They aren't explaining how 2.58 million records were staged and shipped out without triggering a single high-severity alert in their SOC.

I doubt they needed a zero day for this. It was probably just bad credential hygiene at the admin level combined with lateral movement that went unchecked for weeks. If they were running those legacy PHP stacks common in older ISP setups, they might have been hit by the same class of flaws we saw back on October 20 when those two critical PHP vulnerabilities dropped. Did it happen via a known CVE or just a stolen session token? It doesn't really matter. The result is the same.

The response is where Sony actually failed.

Getting hit happens. Being this vague about it is a choice. If you lose data for over 2.5 million people, you should provide immediate transparency to stop the second wave of attacks, and we got corporate prose instead. The data was already indexed by the time the public statement arrived. Attackers didn't wait for a press release to start making money.

The leak itself isn't the most dangerous part; the real threat is the effect on the rest of the Japanese ecosystem. These 2.58 million people use more than one service, and they have government IDs, bank accounts, and logins for e-commerce. This creates a huge window for credential stuffing attacks across other major platforms in the region. The attackers aren't just selling a list. Why would they? They're priming a pump for thousands of smaller intrusions with high value.

Some will argue that Sony followed regulatory guidelines for notification. They might have checked every compliance box required by Japanese law.

Compliance isn't security. A checklist won't stop an attacker from moving laterally through your subnet. Following the law on how to announce a disaster doesn't mean you actually managed that disaster well, and if your strategy is to say as little as possible until you're forced to speak, you aren't managing a breach. You're just documenting your own failure in slow motion.

It's the same pattern we saw with the Everest ransomware group. They recently claimed 590 GB of data from another target. The scale varies, but the arrogance is the same. Both believe that containing the narrative means they can contain the damage. They can't.

The noise on the wire this week has been deafening, and tech and Telecommunications had 352 and 39 stories respectively. Most of it was the PHP2Shell panic. A lean security team can easily get distracted by the flashiest fire. But while everyone watched CISA warn about Node2Shell or PHP bugs, Sony left the back door open long enough for someone to empty the house.

Why do we treat these as "incidents" instead of failures of orchestration? If you can't tell users exactly what was taken and when it happened within 48 hours of detection, your incident response plan is just a piece of paper.

Who else in the So-net and Plala user base has already had their passwords sprayed across other services? I expect account takeovers at Japanese financial institutions will spike over the next ten days.

Sony will eventually release a more detailed report. It will likely blame a "sophisticated actor" to save face. It probably wasn't sophisticated. It was just effective.

Au mois de septembre, le prix du moyen du Brent de la mer du Nord a atteint le deuxième taux le plus élevé de l’année. Ce prix très élevé s’inscrit dans la flambée des cours provoquée par les tensions géopolitiques au Moyen-Orient, notamment la guerre en Iran déclenché par les États-Unis et Israël le 28 février 2026. La stratégie iranienne visant à bloquer le détroit d’Ormuz a fortement réduit l’offre mondiale et a contribué à une reconfiguration des flux pétroliers. Quel est l’état des lieux actuel des marchés pétroliers ? Quels positionnements adoptent l’Organisation des pays exportateurs de pétrole et ses pays alliés (OPEP+), les États-Unis et la Chine ? Face à cette crise, quelle a été la réaction de l’Union européenne (UE) et de quels leviers dispose-t-elle ? Le point avec Francis Perrin, directeur de recherche à l’IRIS.

Le prix du pétrole a atteint au mois de septembre son niveau le plus élevé depuis le mois d’avril. Comment expliquer une telle hausse de prix et quel bilan peut-on dresser de l’impact des conflits au Moyen-Orient sur les marchés pétroliers ?

En septembre, le prix moyen du Brent de la mer du Nord était de 114 dollars (USD) par baril, soit un niveau très élevé. C’est le record en 2026 juste après avril (un peu plus de 117 dollars par baril). Et, sur janvier-septembre, la moyenne (un peu plus de 93 dollars par baril ) est la plus élevée depuis 2022 (100,80 dollars par baril sur 12 mois), année marquée par le début de la seconde guerre en Ukraine. Le 27 octobre, le Brent a clôturé à 114 dollars par baril  environ.

La flambée des prix du pétrole brut et des produits raffinés est la première conséquence de la guerre d’Iran et de la stratégie iranienne visant à bloquer le détroit d’Ormuz, l’un des détroits les plus stratégiques au monde par lequel passent normalement des navires (tankers) transportant de l’ordre de 20 millions de barils par jour de pétrole brut et de produits raffinés. L’Iran a par ailleurs visé et frappé de nombreuses installations énergétiques dans les pays arabes du Golfe, notamment pétrolières et gazières. Outre la hausse des prix, la stratégie iranienne a généré une baisse de la production et des exportations pétrolières du Moyen-Orient, ce qui a réduit l’offre pétrolière mondiale. Cette baisse a été particulièrement forte pour les produits raffinés, notamment le gazole et les carburants avion, dont les prix ont d’ailleurs augmenté beaucoup plus fortement que les prix du brut. Le prix d’un baril de gazole est ainsi quasiment deux fois plus élevé que celui du pétrole… Elle a aussi provoqué une forte baisse des revenus pétroliers des pays arabes du Golfe, pour lesquels le pétrole est évidemment une ressource essentielle, et met gravement en danger leur modèle économique.

Face à cette chute de l’offre pétrolière mondiale, les pays importateurs de pétrole, en tout cas ceux qui ont les moyens de détenir des stocks stratégiques de brut et de produits raffinés, ont mis sur le marché une partie importante de ceux-ci pour limiter la flambée des prix et les risques de pénurie. Il s’agit en particulier des pays membres de l’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE, Paris), qui regroupe 32 États, et de la République populaire de Chine. Les compagnies pétrolières ont quant à elles puisé dans leurs stocks commerciaux. Nowhere does the thesis appear more compelling than in the Gulf region, where states have converted energy, capital, geography and increasingly active roles in mediation into influence far beyond their size. These states have diversified their relationships, expanded their diplomatic reach and have become more willing to resist the preferences of the US, even as Washington continues to maintain the post-Cold War security architecture in the region.Both the UAE and Saudi Arabia engage China and Russia, working closely with both countries on mutual economic and security interests, while retaining their longstanding alliance with Washington. Qatar mediates conflicts involving actors Washington cannot easily reach or engage directly and has expanded ties with China, even as a Major Non-NATO Ally to the US. As Washington has increasingly looked to allies and partners to shoulder more of the burden for addressing challenges to international security, those states have gained greater room to hedge and pursue their own agendas. Modern phishing campaigns can compromise American businesses without relying on traditional credential theft. Attackers can abuse legitimate cloud services, authentication mechanisms, and trusted business workflows to gain access to corporate accounts while leaving fewer obvious signs behind.

ANY.RUN's analysis of Skyw4lker, a device code phishing campaign primarily targeting U.S. organizations, shows how this works in practice. The campaign has focused on manufacturing, technology, and healthcare, using business-themed documents, Google-hosted infrastructure, and Microsoft authentication flows to facilitate account compromise.

For security teams, the investigation goes beyond identifying the initial lure. It requires tracing the authentication flow and supporting infrastructure, extracting reliable indicators, and turning those findings into detections that can protect the wider organization.

Device Code Phishing: A Growing Challenge for U.S. Organizations

The scale of phishing in the United States provides an important backdrop. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded 193,407 phishing and spoofing complaints in 2024, making it one of the most frequently reported categories of internet crime. In 2025, the FBI recorded more than 1 million internet crime complaints and $20.9 billion in reported losses, with reported losses increasing by 26% compared with the previous year.

Attackers are also adapting to organizations that have invested heavily in identity security and MFA.

Device code phishing is one example. Rather than collecting credentials through a fake login page, an attacker can initiate a legitimate device authorization flow and convince the victim to complete it. The resulting authentication tokens can then provide access to resources available to the compromised account.

How Skyw4lker Uses Legitimate Authentication to Compromise Accounts

How the Skyw4lker Campaign Works

Skyw4lker starts with a lure designed to resemble normal business correspondence, as observed in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox analysis.

The Skyw4lker phishing kit identified in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox

Victims receive a password-protected document presented as a contract or service proposal. The scenario is credible in environments where employees routinely exchange vendor agreements, procurement documents, statements of work, and similar files.

From the document, the victim is directed toward a page hosted on sites[.]google[.]com, which eventually leads into a Microsoft authentication flow.

Skyw4lker redirecting the victims to a Microsoft365 authentication page

The attacker does not need to reproduce Microsoft's login experience perfectly. The authentication itself can be legitimate; the deception is in convincing the victim to complete an authentication request initiated by the attacker.

Once the process is completed, the attacker can obtain access to the resulting Microsoft 365 tokens.

That makes the attack difficult to evaluate through identity telemetry alone. An organization may see a valid authentication event without immediately seeing the malicious context that caused it. Establishing what happened requires the security team to connect the document, web activity, authentication flow, and associated infrastructure.

The Infrastructure Behind the Skyw4lker Phishing Page

The web infrastructure used by Skyw4lker provides additional evidence of the campaign's operation.

Denver Health Medical Plan (DHMP) is notifying 238,000 people that their personal and health information may have been compromised in a data breach.

Based in Denver, Colorado, DHMP is a non-profit managed care organization within the Denver Health and Hospital Authority system. Through its Denver Health Medicaid Choice plan, it administers Health First Colorado (Medicaid) benefits for members in Denver and three surrounding counties.

The data breach, DHMP says, involved third-party vendor SquareML, which provides a no-code platform for healthcare analytics.

According to DHMP’s incident notice (PDF), SquareML notified the health plan administrator on August 14, 2026, that an access key was inadvertently leaked on a publicly accessible website.

“These credentials may have been used to access a database maintained by SquareML containing information about DHMP’s 238,083 members,” DHMP says.

The access key was published online on June 27, 2025, and was revoked on August 18, 2026. During this window, it could have been used to access the personal and health information stored in the database.

“The compromised account was read-only, meaning the access key could not be used to download, export, delete, or change any information,” DHMP notes.

The potentially compromised information includes names, dates of birth, ZIP codes, city, state, demographic information, health metrics, health plan eligibility data, hospital admission, provider name, and discharge and transfer data.

According to DHMP, the database did not store Social Security numbers or financial information.

“At this time, DHMP has no evidence that member information was viewed or misused, only that it may have been,” the health plan affiliate notes.

In response to the incident, the passwords for all accounts that had access to the database were reset, and DHMP and SquareML are pursuing additional remedial actions.

Fake login pages are nothing new, but generative AI is making them easier to build and more convincing. Attackers can recreate familiar login screens, impersonate trusted brands and tailor phishing attempts to specific employees or organizations.

Some fake login pages go beyond stealing passwords. They can also capture MFA codes or hijack authenticated sessions, allowing attackers to gain access to corporate accounts even when additional security measures are in place.

How AI is making fake login pages more convincing

Attackers have long used fake login pages to steal credentials, but generative AI makes it easier to create convincing replicas of legitimate authentication portals. From company logos and page layouts to login prompts, these fraudulent pages can closely resemble the websites employees regularly access.

AI also makes it easier to tailor phishing campaigns to specific organizations or employees. For example, attackers can create personalized IT notifications that direct employees to a fraudulent login page using the company's branding and familiar authentication prompts.

These attacks often rely on lookalike domains that closely resemble legitimate web addresses, with subtle spelling changes or additional characters. Combined with realistic login pages and targeted messaging, these tactics make phishing attempts harder to recognize.

While these techniques aren't new, generative AI lets attackers create, customize and adapt phishing campaigns more quickly and at a larger scale. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report found that phishing accounted for 44% of the AI-assisted initial-access techniques examined.

Fake login pages can capture more than usernames and passwords. Some replicate multi-step authentication processes to collect MFA codes, which attackers can attempt to use before they expire to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts and applications.

More sophisticated attacks use Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) techniques to intercept authentication sessions. In these attacks, a fraudulent website acts as a proxy between the user and the legitimate service, relaying authentication requests in real time. After the user successfully authenticates, the attacker may capture a session cookie or authentication token and use it to access the account without completing another MFA challenge.

This makes session hijacking particularly dangerous. Even with MFA enabled, attackers can potentially access accounts by stealing active session tokens. This lets them hijack an authenticated session without entering a password or completing another MFA challenge.

Why traditional phishing defenses aren't always enough

Security awareness training helps employees recognize phishing attempts, but convincing login page replicas can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate websites. Even experienced users can overlook subtle warning signs, particularly when a fraudulent page uses familiar branding and authentication prompts.

Email filters, URL blocklists and website reputation services can stop many known phishing threats, but newly registered domains and short-lived phishing sites may evade detection. Attackers also distribute malicious links through text messages, collaboration platforms and search ads, letting phishing attempts bypass email-based defenses.

URL inspection provides another layer of protection, but lookalike domains can be difficult to identify. A valid HTTPS connection also doesn't guarantee that a website is legitimate.

An attacker who gained access to Keystone's website obtained the key that its hardware wallets use to prove they are genuine, the company said in a statement on October 26.

Someone with that key could build counterfeit devices that pass the online check owners use to verify a Keystone. A buyer who trusted a counterfeit could have their crypto stolen, but the incident did not involve owners' recovery phrases or wallet private keys.

Keystone will destroy 18,835 unsold devices that carry the key, and all new devices will get a new one.

Keystone found the unauthorized access on October 20, and its advice to owners depends on when a device arrived. For a device received after that date with the old key, the company said: "Even if such a device passes authentication, we cannot completely rule out the possibility that it is counterfeit."

Owners of such a device should contact Keystone support and use it only after the company confirms it is genuine.

A device delivered before October 20 that passes the check can be considered genuine and used normally, according to Keystone. The company has not said when the attacker first got in.

The attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool used by Keystone's website to escalate privileges, according to the company. That let the attacker obtain customer data and the key.

Keystone blocked the attacker's access on October 20 and has since fixed the vulnerability. It has not said where the key was stored.

How the Device Check Works

The owner scans a QR code on Keystone's verification page with the device, then enters the code the device displays on the page.

In Keystone's open-source firmware, the QR code carries that code in encrypted form, and the device decrypts it with its stored key. So a correct code shows that the device holds the key.

The key is used only for this check. It plays no part in creating recovery phrases, deriving private keys, or signing transactions.

Anyone with a copy of the key could produce the right codes, so a counterfeit device carrying it could pass the check. Such devices could be sold or shipped to customers, leading to the theft of their crypto, Keystone said. The company has not reported any counterfeit devices or thefts.

The key is written into each device during manufacturing and cannot be erased or rewritten. The firmware keeps it in memory, which can be written only once, and refuses to accept a second key. So devices already made cannot be switched to the new key.

Customer Records

Keystone first disclosed the breach on October 24, saying a third party had obtained customers' shipping information.

The incident affected 25,964 buyer records from purchases on Keystone's website between 2024 and 2026, the company said on October 26. The records hold names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order details. Keystone's online store runs on Shopify, which stored and managed the records.

Payment card and bank details and government ID numbers were not involved, Keystone said. Purchase records from Amazon and Keystone's other sales channels were not affected.

Keystone has also included 12,873 unpaid checkout records in its response as a precaution. These hold names, contact details, and shipping information from purchases that were never completed.

Some of the affected data should already have been deleted. Keystone had promised to delete shipping information 180 days after each order.

An automated tool Keystone built to erase records in bulk did not work reliably. Some deletions failed, and Keystone did not catch the failures in time.
